Getting started with imbalanceKit

Fatih Sağlam

2026-10-29

imbalanceKit.Rmd

imbalanceKit brings resampling methods, performance metrics and data complexity measures for imbalanced classification together. This article walks through a typical workflow on the banana data: look at the problem, resample, post-process the synthetic samples with DatRel, and check whether it helps a classifier.

library(imbalanceKit)

The data

banana is a two-dimensional data set with a minority (positive) class that overlaps with the majority class. It contains the usual difficulties of imbalanced data: a small minority class, class overlap, noise and small disjuncts.

x <- banana[, c("At1", "At2")]
y <- banana$Class
table(y)
#> y
#> negative positive 
#>     2376      264

All resamplers take a numeric feature matrix (or data frame) x and a factor class variable y. A small helper for the plots of this article:

col_neg <- "#9aa5b1"
col_pos <- "#c0392b"
col_syn <- "#1f6fb2"

plot_classes <- function(x, y, x_syn = NULL, main = "") {
  x <- as.matrix(x)
  plot(x, type = "n", xlab = "At1", ylab = "At2", main = main, asp = 1)
  if (!is.null(x_syn)) {
    points(as.matrix(x_syn), col = adjustcolor(col_syn, 0.45), pch = 17, cex = 0.5)
  }
  neg <- y != "positive"
  points(x[neg, , drop = FALSE], col = col_neg, pch = 1, cex = 0.5)
  points(x[!neg, , drop = FALSE], col = col_pos, pch = 16, cex = 0.6)
}

par(mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
plot_classes(x, y, main = "banana")

How hard is the problem?

complexity() measures class imbalance, class overlap and noise. Every measure is also available as its own function, for example complexity_IR().

complexity(x, y, measures = c("IR", "R", "R_aug", "N1", "N3", "N4"), seed = 1)
#>         IR          R      R_aug         N1         N3         N4 
#> 9.00000000 0.03750000 0.27689394 0.08219697 0.05757576 0.25000000

IR is the imbalance ratio. R and R_aug describe how much of the data lies in the overlap region, and R_aug weighs the classes by their sizes so that the minority class is not drowned. N1, N3 and N4 are neighbourhood based measures of class overlap and noise. See ?complexity_measures for all of them.

Oversampling

SMOTE() creates synthetic minority samples between neighbouring minority samples. The result is a list.

set.seed(1)
m <- SMOTE(x, y)
names(m)
#> [1] "x_new" "y_new" "x_syn" "y_syn"
table(m$y_new)
#> 
#> negative positive 
#>     2376     2376

x_new and y_new are the original data plus the synthetic samples, which are also returned alone as x_syn and y_syn. ovRate = 1 (the default) balances the classes; a smaller value generates fewer samples.

Methods of this package can be swapped freely because they share the interface. Here are four of them on the same data (minority samples in red, synthetic samples in blue):

set.seed(1)
res <- list(
  SMOTE    = SMOTE(x, y),
  BLSMOTE  = BLSMOTE(x, y),
  BiSMOTE  = BiSMOTE(x, y),
  SMOTEWB  = SMOTEWB(x, y)
)

par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
for (nm in names(res)) {
  plot_classes(x, y, res[[nm]]$x_syn, main = nm)
}

The methods differ mainly in where they place the samples; the overlap region between the classes is where they differ most.

Post-processing with DatRel

DatRel is not a resampler by itself: it takes samples from any source and moves the ones that fall outside the region of their class back into it. The region is a set of balls, centred at a few dominating samples, that do not contain a sample of another class.

set.seed(1)
m <- SMOTE(x, y)
d <- DatRel(x, y, x_syn = m$x_syn, y_syn = m$y_syn)
d$n_relocated
#> $positive
#> [1] 295

295 of the 2112 synthetic samples were outside the minority region and were relocated. The plot shows those samples (orange) before and after the relocation:

moved <- rowSums(abs(m$x_syn - d$x_syn)) > 0

par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
plot_classes(x, y, m$x_syn[!moved, ], main = "SMOTE")
points(m$x_syn[moved, ], col = "#e67e22", pch = 17, cex = 0.6)
plot_classes(x, y, d$x_syn[!moved, ], main = "SMOTE + DatRel")
points(d$x_syn[moved, ], col = "#e67e22", pch = 17, cex = 0.6)

oversampleDatRel() does both steps with a base method of your choice, for example oversampleDatRel(x, y, method = "BiSMOTE").

Does it help a classifier?

Resampling is only applied to the training data. Here a decision tree is trained on the original training data, on SMOTE and on SMOTE + DatRel, and compared on held-out test data over 10 random stratified splits. evaluate() calculates several metrics at once.

split_data <- function(y, p_train = 0.7) {
  idx <- unlist(lapply(split(seq_along(y), y), function(i) {
    i[sample.int(length(i), round(p_train * length(i)))]
  }))
  sort(idx)
}

fit_eval <- function(x_train, y_train, x_test, y_test) {
  fit <- rpart::rpart(y ~ ., data = data.frame(x_train, y = y_train))
  pred <- predict(fit, data.frame(x_test), type = "class")
  evaluate(y_test, y_pred = pred, positive = "positive",
           metrics = c("BACC", "GMEAN", "F1", "MCC"))
}

set.seed(2026)
results <- lapply(1:10, function(r) {
  i_train <- split_data(y)
  x_tr <- x[i_train, ]; y_tr <- y[i_train]
  x_te <- x[-i_train, ]; y_te <- y[-i_train]

  s <- SMOTE(x_tr, y_tr)
  d <- DatRel(x_tr, y_tr, s$x_syn, s$y_syn)

  rbind(
    original         = fit_eval(x_tr, y_tr, x_te, y_te),
    SMOTE            = fit_eval(s$x_new, s$y_new, x_te, y_te),
    `SMOTE + DatRel` = fit_eval(d$x_new, d$y_new, x_te, y_te)
  )
})

round(Reduce(`+`, results) / length(results), 3)
#>                 BACC GMEAN    F1   MCC
#> original       0.814 0.796 0.695 0.667
#> SMOTE          0.859 0.858 0.599 0.569
#> SMOTE + DatRel 0.860 0.859 0.601 0.573

The table shows the mean of the 10 splits. Balancing the classes raises the metrics that treat both classes equally (BACC, GMEAN) but can lower F1 and MCC, because more majority samples are classified as positive. Which method wins depends on the data and the classifier, so compare several methods and several classifiers on your own problem; the metrics of evaluate() are described in ?metrics.
